parts:
The following code:

t1 <-data.frame(n=factor(rep(1:2,1,each=60)),X = 1:100)
t1$Y1 <- runif(t1$X)
t1$Y2 <- runif(t1$X)*100000
t1 <-t1[,-2]
str(t1)
ggplot(data=t1)+geom_histogram(aes(x=Y1))
ggplot(data=t1)+geom_histogram(aes(x=Y1))


m1 <-melt(t1, ids="n")

ggplot2(data=m1)+geom_histogram(aes(x=value))+facet_grid(value~.)

Yields many error reports of this type:

stat_bin: binwidth defaulted to range/30. Use 'binwidth = x' to adjust this.

Hmmm. I had to tweak your code a bit to get it to run at all:

## next line fails in original form: changed X from '1:100' to '1:120'
t1 <-data.frame(n=factor(rep(1:2,1,each=60)),X = 1:120)

t1$Y1 <- runif(t1$X)
t1$Y2 <- runif(t1$X)*100000
t1 <-t1[,-2]
str(t1)

## why not:
t1 <- data.frame(n=factor(rep(1:2,each=60)),Y1=runif(120),
Y2=runif(120)*1e5)

library(ggplot2)
ggplot(data=t1)+geom_histogram(aes(x=Y1))
## next line was identical. Did you mean to plot Y2 instead?
ggplot(data=t1)+geom_histogram(aes(x=Y2))
m1 <-melt(t1, ids="n")

# ============

The messages are not errors, they are warnings.
I think what's happening is that you are asking R to plot 120 separate
rows, *one for each value of the data* (i.e. each histogram has a single
value in it). Since ggplot is slow at faceting, this takes longer than
you are willing to wait. Try

t2 <- data.frame(n=factor(rep(1:2,each=5)),Y1=runif(10),
Y2=runif(10)*1e5)
ggplot(data=melt(t2,ids="n"))+geom_histogram(aes(x=value))+facet_grid(value~.)

Is this what you meant? I think you might have preferred

## changed ggplot2 to ggplot
ggplot(data=m1)+geom_histogram(aes(x=value))+facet_grid(variable~.)

I would consider it a bit of a limitation of ggplot2 (despite its
general wonderfulness) that it does not allow any simple way to set
non-default binwidths that are *different* in each facet. Hadley would
probably say that this is a feature; faceting is designed to display
multiple subsets of the same data in small multiples. What we are doing
here is an "off-label" (in the pharmaceutical sense) approach to fitting
multiple different variables, each in its own facet. Since it conflicts
with the design philosophy of ggplot2, it's harder to achieve.

cheers
Ben Bolker

parts: Hi,

On Mon, Jan 17, 2011 at 12:55 PM, Rob James <r...@aetiologic.ca> wrote:
> The following code:
>
> t1 <-data.frame(n=factor(rep(1:2,1,each=60)),X = 1:100)
> t1$Y1 <- runif(t1$X)
> t1$Y2 <- runif(t1$X)*100000
> t1 <-t1[,-2]
> str(t1)
> ggplot(data=t1)+geom_histogram(aes(x=Y1))
> ggplot(data=t1)+geom_histogram(aes(x=Y1))
>
>
> m1 <-melt(t1, ids="n")
>
> ggplot2(data=m1)+geom_histogram(aes(x=value))+facet_grid(value~.)

What you are doing here is asking for:

length(unique(m1$value))

facets. Is that really what you wanted or were you deliberately
trying to make it crash?

>
> Yields many error reports of this type:
>
> stat_bin: binwidth defaulted to range/30. Use 'binwidth = x' to adjust this.

These are not errors, just notes from ggplot about what it is doing.
The reason there are so many is that you are faceting so many times.

>
> and then a consistent loss of control to R

ggplot2 is not the fastest thing ever, and you just asked it for 200
something histograms faceted into some monstrous display. If you want
that, you'll need a powerful system and some patience.

Perhaps you meant:

ggplot(data = m1) + geom_histogram(aes(x = value)) +
facet_grid(. ~ variable + n)

? or some variant of that?

Cheers,

Josh

Ben,

Thanks, a crash and a long delay often look similar. Your revised code
showed the problem with which I was grappling.
As Joshua and you both noted, I mis-specified what I wanted.

You make a great point. If ggplot allowed this then you could do
something like Harrell's describe package in the rms library, but avoid
the LATEX overhead - a simple visual data screening tool. It would be
very valuable for this purpose, amongst others, but clearly exceeds the
design at this time.

Hadley, is this a possible feature, or does it run against the grain?

implemented elsewhere (ggextra?). In some ways, it does not seem like
